To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the star formation law in the disk of the galaxy NGC 5194 is well fit by a power-law of slope 0.82, with an intrinsic scatter of 0.43 dex, and a typical depletion timescales tau=SIGMA {sub H{sub 1+H{sub2}}}/SIGM{sub SFR}{approx}2 Gyr.

the star formation rate surface density (SIGMAMSFR) in the disk of the Whirlpool Galaxy (M51a) correlates with the surface density of molecular gas, SIGMASFR = 0.83 SIGMASFR + 0.43 dex, with a scatter of 0.43 in the log of SIGMA SFR, and that the star formation efficiency (the inverse of the depletion timescale) is constant at 0.5 Gyr.

we have used integral field spectroscopy to measure the SFR and gas surface densities in 735 regions in the central part of NGC 5194 with an angular resolution similar to 170 pc, and we have found a linear SFL with slope N=0.82+-0.05 and an intrinsic scatter of 0.43+-0.02 dex, and a typical depletion timescales of 2 Gyr for the molecular gas component.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of new techniques to the study of the structure and dynamics of the interstellar media of galaxies.
the development of novel methods to study and understand the physics of the ISM in nearby galaxies.
the study of the formation of the most massive stars in the Milky Way, in particular the formation of the massive star cluster RCW 38.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the star formation law is not linear.
the SFR is a complex function of the gas surface density.
the SFL is a well established and robust relation, but its slope, and the role of the gas phase, are still under discussion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the star formation rate is not a linear function of the gas density.
we use a new fitting method that is able to account for the intrinsic scatter in a relation, and that we use it to measure the SFL in the Whirlpool galaxy.
our results support the recent finding that the star formation rate surface density (SIGMASFR) and the gas surface density (SIGMAG) are linearly related.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the SFR is a strong function of SIGMA{sub H2}, with a slope close to 1 and a scatter in the SFL of about 0.5 dex, but the atomic component of the gas is not correlated with the SFR.
the star formation law is not a linear function of gas density.
we can use the SFL to estimate the SFR of a galaxy, and the depletion time scale of its interstellar medium, provided that we have a good measurement of the total molecular gas mass surface density.
